messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.body_plain:
its only an 'error' in the sense that the input is wrong or
inconsistent, and the code detect that and cannot move on. it should be
easy to fix if understanding the issue at hand.

if you have a regional model like besag (not bym, which make less sense
in this context), then you cannot make it orthogonal to covariates,
unless you have one covariate pr region. with several pr region you have
to define how to make it 'in average' orthogonal.

Best
H

On Thu, 2021-04-29 at 13:55 -0700, John Molitor wrote:
> Thanks again for this. All is fine with the iid model, but when I use
> a spatial model (e.g. bym or besag) using your code, I again get a
> dimension error, even using "values=1:N".
>
> I suppose the dimension of the graph is an issue? Note that A has N
> columns while the graph will have size of num.grp.
>
> Of course it will work if I create an A matrix derived from an X
> matrix with binned covariate values so the number of rows of X equals
> num.grp. This can be achieve by using, within each grp, median values
> for continuous covariates or perhaps modal values for categorical
> covariates. However it would seem that I would lose a lot of
> information this way.
>
> John
>
>
> On Thursday, April 29, 2021 at 2:41:17 AM UTC-7 he...@r-inla.org
> wrote:
> >
> > this is also related to the post
> >  [r-inla] Modelling continuous covariates using RW2 latent model
> >
> > about 'values', which defines for which values the model is defined
> > for.
> > you need to control this yourself, like I do in the code. Its easy
> > if
> > num.grp is eq to N, but I guess you can revert some of the changes I
> > did
> > (which I thought caused the problems), before realising that the
> > random
> > dimension of the iid model was the issue.
> >
> > H
> >
> > On Wed, 2021-04-28 at 22:30 -0700, John Molitor wrote:
> > > Thank you very much for this. Regarding adding a constraint to
> > > implement Restricted Spatial Regression (RSR), I'm a little
> > > confused
> > > about dimension issues. Here's some code for a super simple iid
> > model.
> > > (I know that RSR is not really needed here, I'm just trying to
> > > understand coding issues.)
> > >
> > > I'm simply fitting:
> > >
> > > y_i = alpha_(r_i) + beta*x + error_i, where r_i=r, the region to
> > which
> > > individual i belongs.
> > >
> > > alpha_r = alpha.0 + error_alpha_r
> > >
> > > --------------------------------------------------
> > >
> > > require(INLA)
> > >
> > > rm(list=ls())
> > > set.seed(1)
> > >
> > > N <- 100
> > >
> > > num.grps <- 10
> > > grp <- sample(1:num.grps,N,rep=T)
> > >
> > > sd.alpha <- 1
> > > alpha.0 <- 3
> > > alphas <- rnorm(num.grps,alpha.0,sd.alpha)
> > >
> > > beta <- 0.2
> > >
> > > x <- rnorm(N)
> > > y <- alphas[grp] + beta * x + rnorm(N,sd=0.1)
> > >
> > > dat <- data.frame(x,y)
> > >
> > > require(INLA)
> > > f <- y ~ 1 + f(grp,model="iid") + x
> > > mod.inla <- inla(f,data=dat)
> > >
> > > X <- mod.inla$model.matrix
> > >
> > > P <- X %*% solve(t(X)%*%X) %*% t(X)
> > > A.rsr <- diag(nrow(P)) - P
> > > e.rsr <- rep(0,nrow(A.rsr))
> > >
> > > f.rsr <- y ~ 1 + f(grp,
> > >                    extraconstr=list(A=as.matrix(A.rsr),
> > >                                     e=rep(0,nrow(A.rsr))),
> > >                    ) + x
> > >
> > >
> > > ## Dimension Error
> > > mod.inla.rst <- inla(f.rsr,data=dat)
> > >

messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much for this! I got it all to work by averaging in the manner stated previously to create "average" orthogonality. Results seem reasonable.

If you could bear one more question: Does this approach work for the slopes, where the formula is of the form "...x + f(idx, x,...)"? Note my A matrix (for extraconstr) has x in it (as x is a covariate in the model) while x is also a weight in the besag random effect.

John

On Sun, 2021-05-02 at 21:18 -0700, John Molitor wrote:
> Thanks so much for this! I got it all to work by averaging in the
> manner stated previously to create "average" orthogonality. Results

> If you could bear one more question: Does this approach work for the
> slopes, where the formula is of the form "...x + f(idx, x,...)"? Note
> my A matrix (for extraconstr) has x in it (as x is a covariate in the
> model) while x is also a weight in the besag random effect.

yes, that should be fine. '+x' is linear in 'x' and by having weights
'x' with coefficients in f(idx...), then you say you do not want that
confounding.

one simple example is

	x + f(time, x, model="rw2"...)

for which [1, x] spans the null-space of 'rw2', and then you really need
it.

H

messages.subject: Stochastic volatility models in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi there! I am a brand new user of INLA. It is a great package, love it! :)

I am working with GARCH models (already implemented in INLA, see for instance this interesting paper <https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/1351847X.2010.495475>) and not find any 'inspirational example' to understand/see how to implement and fit these models in R. I found a link to a tutorial (in particular StochVol study case) <https://sites.google.com/a/r-inla.org/www/examples/volume-ii?authuser=0>, but the links to code is missing. Could you please provide the the previous mentioned study case (or any other equivalent case study) developed in R, I would greatly appreciate it!

Thanks
Gabriel

messages.body_plain:
Ugh, I still have one more technical question. You've been very helpful and I appreciate it.

To establish "average orthogonality" my A matrix consists of mean values of continuous covariates per grp, and modal values of categorical covariates per group (with random selection when there are more than one mode).

For an original categorical covariate, x_cat, there may be 4 levels, 1,2,3,4. However, in the A matrix,  I may end up with only three values for this covariate, 1,2,4. Does this mess things up? Will the categories for x_cat in the A matrix (3 levels) correspond to levels for the same covariate in the data with four levels, 1,2,3,4? Or will things get relabeled somehow?

John

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Stochastic volatility models in INLA
messages.body_plain:
Stoch vol models is nothing else than a special likelihood, where the
unknown process in time drives the variance of Gaussian noise. usually,
its linear in log(variance) [or log(stdev) og log(prec), which are all
the same]. for the latent model, then AR1, or AR1C (with covaraiates)
are used.

I attach some simple examples you might find useful. as always, the only
way to make sure you do the right thing, is to simulate data and
estimate them back [and getting the parameters back of'course]

H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] SVC models - dueling BYM's?
messages.body_plain:
to make the spatial field orthogonal to covariates, then if its a
continous indexed field (model=spde), then only continous covariates
should be considered and only those can could have been measured
everywhere.

with a region model, then its a little different, and you can make it
orthogonal to covariates that are region spesific. and this, I guess,
could include factors as well.

if you have factors in the formula, then these are expanded and
sometimes reduced (like lm() does), [there is an alternative expansion
in 'expand.factor.strategy' in control.fixed], so I guess as you say,
this can create issues. as long as you have the same levels included in
both places, it should go fine [as the correction should be invariant to
the levels]. But if you have level 1,2,3 in the correction, and 1,2,3,4
in the model itself, then there could be an issue.

the only way (beyond the new strategy as mention) to control the
expansion of factors, is to do it yourself, by recoding factors into
vectors of numerics.

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have an additional question related to this, in the adjacency matrix, is it ok to have the same id more than once in the same raw?
ex

3
1 2 2 3
2 2 1 3 3

3 2 1 2 1

On Saturday, April 24, 2021 at 10:38:27 PM UTC+5:30 guna...@umn.edu wrote:
> Ok , Thanks a lot,   I think I understand what you are saying,  I should make a new adjacency matrix fulfilling the above criteria,
>
> Thanks
> Umanga
>

> >

> > 3 2 1 2

> > 3 1 2
> >

messages.subject_clean: combined analysis of point-level and area-level data using SPDE
messages.body_plain:
Depending on exactly what your data look like you might be interested in:

This paper fits areal and point data. It uses INLA and then switches to TMB for later models.
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30202860/

My paper here where we use areal and point data on different scales (prevalence and incidence) using TMB. Also the references in the intro might be useful.
https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/rssc.12484

Sorry for the self-plug.

Tim

messages.subject: Spatial data in shapefile grid: ID problems
messages.subject_clean: Spatial data in shapefile grid: ID problems
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I'm following a Coding Club tutorial (https://ourcodingclub.github.io/tutorials/spatial-modelling-inla/) and adapting my own data.

My problems may be coming from the ID column which is a list of 1834 unique IDs, not starting at 1 (i.e. 2, 3, 4, 8 ....2053). The lattice has 1834 squares. My code is:

lattice <- readOGR("grid_with_points.shp")
data <- lattice@data # first variable is 'ID' = chr
Lattice_Temp <- poly2nb(lattice, row.names = data$ID)
nb2INLA("Lattice.graph", Lattice_Temp)
Lattice.adj <- "Lattice.graph"
data$ID <- as.numeric(data$ID)

formula <- NUMPOINTS ~ NGcost_mea + elev_mean + elev_min + elev_max +
  X1_mean + X2_mean + X3_mean + X4_mean + X5_mean + X6_mean + X7_mean +
  X8_mean + X9_mean + X10_mean + X11_mean + X12_mean + X13_mean + X14_mean +   X15_mean + X16_mean + X17_mean + X18_mean + X19_mean + X21_mean + X22_mean +   X23_mean + X24_mean + X25_mean + X26_mean + X27_mean + X28_mean + X29_mean +   X30_mean + X31_mean + X32_mean + X33_mean + X34_mean + X35_mean + X36_mean +   X37_mean + X38_mean + X39_mean + X40_mean + X41_mean + X42_mean + X43_mean +   X44_mean + X45_mean + X46_mean + f(ID, model = "bym", graph = Lattice.adj)

Mod_Lattice <- inla(formula,
                    family = "poisson",
                    data = data,
                    control.compute = list(cpo = T, dic = T, waic = T))

I get " f(ID). Covariate does not match 'values' 177 times. Indexes for mismatch:929 930 [...etc...] 1834. This is not what you want. Use NA values in the covariate"

Yet if I leave ID as a 'chr' field I get this instead: "In f(ID): 'covariate' must match 'values',  and both must either be 'numeric', or 'factor'/'character'." Scylla and Charybdis....

Looking at the helpfile for poly2nb, it seems a character vector is expected for the region.id <http://region.id>. I tried setting it as numeric: no immediate problem, but I still get the 'covariate does not match' error.  I tried not setting row.names at all - this gives me a region.id <http://region.id> of 1:1834 but the same error.

Does anyone have any advice? And what's that about NA values?

messages.subject_clean: INLA implementation for I00K non-Gaussian point-referenced data
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am trying to implement INLA for massive non-Gaussian point-referenced data (n=100K). When I made a mesh, I used cutoff=0.05 and it takes about 10 hours from my personal desktop.

To make this faster, I made a fewer number of the mesh by changing cutoff=0.1 (Please see the following code). However, this choice of cutoff makes an error message. The followings are part of my code.

#############################################################
## Define Mesh using Coordinates
 observations lower-center area of map
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(gridLocation, max.edge=c(1,1),cutoff=0.1)  # no error at 0.05
AMat <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=gridLocation)
AMatCV <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=predLocation)
dim(AMat)

# Model fitting
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh=mesh, alpha=2)
stk.e <- inla.stack(tag='est', ## tag
                    data=list(y=Z), ## response
                    A=list(AMat, 1), ## two projector matrix
                    effects=list(## two elements:
                      s=1:spde$n.spde, ## RF index
                      data.frame( x1=XMat[,1],x2=XMat[,2])))
# Prediction fitting
stk.pred <- inla.stack(tag='pred', A=list(AMatCV, 1),
                       data=list(y=NA), ## response as NA
                       effects=list(s=1:spde$n.spde,
                                    data.frame(x1=Xpreds[,1],x2=Xpreds[,2])))

stk.full <- inla.stack(stk.e, stk.pred)
formula <- y ~ 0  + x1 + x2 +## fixed part
             f(s, model=spde) ## RF term
link = c(rep(NA, n),rep(1, n.pred))
res<-inla(formula,
          data=inla.stack.data(stk.full, spde=spde),
          family="binomial",  #binomial, poisson

Dear all,

I am new to R-inla. I am running spatio-temporal model with interactions for disease mapping. Thanks advance
ssubra
---

require(lattice)
require(abind)
library(rgdal)
library(spdep)
library(dplyr)
library(RColorBrewer)
library(ggplot2)
library(ggregplot)

prec_space <- list(c(1, 0.00048684), c(1, 0.00194738), c(1, 0.04868439), c(1, 0.00005))
prec_interact <- list(c(1, 0.00078138), c(1, 0.00312552), c(1, 0.07813805), c(1, 0.00005))
prec_interact2 <- list(c(1,0.00040145), c(1, 0.00160580), c(1, 0.04014488), c(1, 0.00005))

##############import shapefile#########################
#shp <- readOGR(dsn = "H:/blockmapVl", layer = "blockmapVL") #491 BLOCKS

shp <- readOGR(dsn = "D:/VL model/502 blocks/shp", layer = "merged_bihar") #502 BLOCKS

# define adjacency matrix for spatial model
nb <- poly2nb(shp)

# translate to INLA format and save

  +f(block.period,model="iid",hyper = prec_interact)

  f(period_id2,model="iid",hyper = prec_period) +f(block_id2,model="iid", group=period_id3,control.group=list(model="rw1"),hyper = prec_interact)

mod.intII1 <- inla(formula.intII1,family="nbinomial",data=data,offset=log(E2),# changed from 'pop' to 'E'
                   control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-9, diagonal=10, strategy="laplace"),

mod.intIII1 <- inla(formula.intIII1,family="nbinomial",data=data,offset=log(E2),# changed from 'pop' to 'E'

formula.intIII2<- count ~  1+Maximum_temp+EVI+Minimum_temp+BIO.1+BIO.3+BIO.12+popdens+Soil_moisture +
  f(block_id,model="bym",graph=g,hyper = prec_space) +f(period_id,model="rw2",hyper = prec_period) +

messages.subject: How to recover the local variance and range from a non-stationary model.
messages.subject_clean: How to recover the local variance and range from a non-stationary model.
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

I am trying to recover the local variance and range based on posterior sampling and transformations but I am wondering a) if the code presented bellow is the way to go, and b) if there is a direct way to do it similarly to the stationary case ( when inla.spde2.pcmatern is used instead).

Assume the local precision varies and range is constant as follows:

log(k) = log(k_0) + theta1,

log(tau_s) = log(tau_0) + theta2 + theta3*b(s),

for given log(k_0), log(tau_0) and theta1, theta2, theta3 hyper-parameters with appropriate priors where b(s) is a monotone function evaluated on the mesh nodes s.

For my toy example I am using the following code to define the spde:

spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh,

B.kappa = cbind( log(k_0), 1, 0, 0),

B.tau = cbind( log(tau_0), 0, 1, b_s)),

theta.prior.mean = rep(0, 3),

theta.prior.prec = rep(1, 3))

b_s is a vector with values from a monotone function b(s) evaluated on the mesh nodes.

I generate a posterior sample for the hyper-parameters theta using the function inla.hyperpar.sample and store it in

hyperSamples .

Next I transform the posterior sample as follows to obtain the range and local nominal variance:

kappa = exp(hyperSamples[, 1])

tau_ns = exp(cbind(1, b_s))%*%t(hyperSamples[, 2:3]))

rho = sqrt(8)/kappa

sigma2_ns = (4*pi*kappa^2*tau_ns^2)^(-1)

Is the above approach correct in order to obtain the nominal spatial variance and range, or am I missing any key components linked with the inner parametrizations or with the numerical approximations involved in the process?

Thank you in advance for any insights.

Best regards,

Christos.

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to recover the local variance and range from a non-stationary model.
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

For the nominal model variances in an estimated SPDE model, see inla.spde.posterior().
For the actual model variances, you can compute it for given theta values via
Q<-inla.spde.precision(model, theta)
variance<-diag(inla.qinv(Q))
You can combine that with posterior samples of theta if you want e.g. the posterior expectation of the model variances.

Finn

messages.subject: specification of random slope models
messages.body_plain:
Could someone help me understand the difference between the two specifications below, where the aim is to induce a random slope on the covariate X? I've seen both specifications for random slopes in the literature on INLA. Is the difference that Model 2 says that everything about the slope is random, whereas Model 1 says that there's a common (fixed) component in addition to the random one?  If so, then absent a strong theory, why would one want to use Model 2, since if it's correct, then the coefficient on X in Model 1 ought to be revealed as essentially zero?

The two specifications:

Model 1: y~1+ X + f(id,X,model="iid)
Model 2: y~1 + f(id,X, model="iid)

(The, difference is that the first specification includes X among the fixed covariates, while the second doesn't).

Thanks for any help on this!

On Sun, 2021-05-09 at 09:40 -0700, vit...@osu.edu wrote:
> Could someone help me understand the difference between the two
> specifications below, where the aim is to induce a random slope on the
> covariate X?

There is also a the model 'intslope' that simplifies the spesification
of a random intercept-slope model (when it applies)

> I've seen both specifications for random slopes in the
> literature on INLA. Is the difference that Model 2 says that
> everything
> about the slope is random, whereas Model 1 says that there's a common
> (fixed) component in addition to the random one?  If so, then absent a
> strong theory, why would one want to use Model 2, since if it's
> correct,
> then the coefficient on X in Model 1 ought to be revealed as
> essentially
> zero?
>
> The two specifications:
>
> Model 1: y~1+ X + f(id,X,model="iid)

this is an overparameterisation and gives a lin.predictor as

	intercept + beta * x  + u(id) * x

where 'u(id)' is the random intercept. in the case where id=1:n, f.ex,
then you can move a constant from 'beta' to the u's, hence the
overparametersation.

you may add

	f(id, X, model="iid", constr=TRUE)

then u(id)'s will sum to zero, hence the 'beta' will be the average
effect, and the 'u(id)'s the variations around it.

> Model 2: y~1 + f(id,X, model="iid)
>

this is

	intercept + u(id) * x

only, where the u(id)'s have a common (and unknown) precision

messages.subject: Running a zero-altered Poisson (ZAP) model n R-inla
messages.subject_clean: Running a zero-altered Poisson (ZAP) model n R-inla
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to run a ZAP model in inla and I keep getting this error:

Error in inla(fZA.mesh1, family = c("zeroinflatedpoisson0", "binomial"),  :
  Number of families 2 does not match number of response variables 1492

Here is my code below:

# 19.7 ZAP model with spatial correlation

# 19.7.1 Running the model in R-INLA
UG4$Species01  <- ifelse(UG4$total_deaths==0, 0, 1) # Presence/absence part
UG4$SpeciesPos <- ifelse(UG4$total_deaths > 0, UG4$total_deaths, NA) # count part

# Spatial index for count part
w1.pos.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'wpos', n.spde  = spde1$n.spde)
# Spatial index for presence/absence part
w1.01.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'w01', n.spde  = spde1$n.spde)

Xm <- model.matrix(~bio6.std + bio18.std + elevation.std +
                     distance.water.std +s.pH.std + s.calcium.std + s.carbon.std +
                     s.water.std + mean.ndvi.std,
                   data = UG4)

N <- nrow(UG4)
X <- data.frame(Intercept  = rep(1, N),
                bio6.std             = Xm[, 2],
                bio18.std            = Xm[, 3],
                elevation.std        = Xm[, 4],
                distance.water.std   = Xm[, 5],
                s.pH.std             = Xm[, 6],
                s.calcium.std        = Xm[, 7],
                s.carbon.std         = Xm[, 8],
                s.water.std          = Xm[, 9],
                mean.ndvi.std        = Xm[, 10])

X01 <- data.frame(Intercept.01         = rep(1, N),
                  bio6.std.01             = Xm[, 2],
                  bio18.std.01            = Xm[, 3],
                  elevation.std.01        = Xm[, 4],
                  distance.water.std.01   = Xm[, 5],
                  s.pH.std.01             = Xm[, 6],
                  s.calcium.std.01        = Xm[, 7],
                  s.carbon.std.01         = Xm[, 8],
                  s.water.std.01          = Xm[, 9],
                  mean.ndvi.std.01        = Xm[, 10])

# And this is the stack for the ZAP model
StackPos.mesh1 <- inla.stack(
  tag  = "FitPos",
  data = list(AllY = cbind(UG4$SpeciesPos, NA)),
  A    = list(1, A1),
  effects = list(
    Xpos = as.data.frame(X),
    wpos = w1.pos.index))

Stack01.mesh1 <- inla.stack(
  tag  = "Fit01",
  data = list(AllY = cbind(NA, UG4$Species01)),
  A    = list(1, A1),
  effects = list(
    X01 = as.data.frame(X01),
    w01 = w1.01.index))

Stack.ZA.mesh1 <- inla.stack(StackPos.mesh1, Stack01.mesh1)

# Specify the model formula
fZA.mesh1  <- AllY ~ -1 + Intercept + bio6.std + bio18.std + elevation.std +
  distance.water.std +s.pH.std + s.calcium.std + s.carbon.std +
  s.water.std + mean.ndvi.std +
  f(wpos, model = spde1) +

  Intercept.01 + bio6.std.01 + bio18.std.01 + elevation.std.01 +
  distance.water.std.01 +s.pH.std.01 + s.calcium.std.01 + s.carbon.std.01 +
  s.water.std.01 + mean.ndvi.std.01 +
  f(w01, model = spde1)

# Run model
HyperZap <- list(theta = list(initial = -10, fixed = TRUE)) # For zero-truncated
ZAP.mesh1 <- inla(fZA.mesh1,
                  family = c("zeroinflatedpoisson0", "binomial"),
                  control.family = list(list(hyper = HyperZap),
                                        list()),
                  data = inla.stack.data(Stack.ZA.mesh1),
                  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                  control.predictor = list(
                    link = 1,
                    A = inla.stack.A(Stack.ZA.mesh1)))

Many thanks in advance.

Best regards,
Valentina.

Hi Elias,

At first I ran it and got 'NULL" results for both, but then I re-ran the entire code and got the following results:

> str(cbind(UG4$SpeciesPos, NA))
 int [1:746, 1:2] 1 8 2 1 3 7 2 1 1 1 ...
> str(cbind(NA, UG4$Species01))
 num [1:746, 1:2] NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA NA ...

Many thanks for the clue.

Kind regards,
Valentina.

> > Hi,
> >
> > I am trying to run a ZAP model in inla and I keep getting this error:
> >
> > Error in inla(fZA.mesh1, family = c("zeroinflatedpoisson0", "binomial"),  :
> >   Number of families 2 does not match number of response variables 1492
> >
> > Here is my code below:
> >
> > # 19.7 ZAP model with spatial correlation
> >
> >
> > # 19.7.1 Running the model in R-INLA
> > UG4$Species01  <- ifelse(UG4$total_deaths==0, 0, 1) # Presence/absence part
> > UG4$SpeciesPos <- ifelse(UG4$total_deaths > 0, UG4$total_deaths, NA) # count part
> >
> > # Spatial index for count part
> > w1.pos.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'wpos', n.spde  = spde1$n.spde)
> > # Spatial index for presence/absence part
> > w1.01.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = 'w01', n.spde  = spde1$n.spde)
> >
> >
> > Xm <- model.matrix(~bio6.std + bio18.std + elevation.std +
> >                      distance.water.std +s.pH.std + s.calcium.std + s.carbon.std +
> >                      s.water.std + mean.ndvi.std,
> >                    data = UG4)
> >
> > N <- nrow(UG4)
> > X <- data.frame(Intercept  = rep(1, N),
> >                 bio6.std             = Xm[, 2],
> >                 bio18.std            = Xm[, 3],
> >                 elevation.std        = Xm[, 4],
> >                 distance.water.std   = Xm[, 5],
> >                 s.pH.std             = Xm[, 6],
> >                 s.calcium.std        = Xm[, 7],
> >                 s.carbon.std         = Xm[, 8],
> >                 s.water.std          = Xm[, 9],
> >                 mean.ndvi.std        = Xm[, 10])
> >
> >
> > X01 <- data.frame(Intercept.01         = rep(1, N),
> >                   bio6.std.01             = Xm[, 2],
> >                   bio18.std.01            = Xm[, 3],
> >                   elevation.std.01        = Xm[, 4],
> >                   distance.water.std.01   = Xm[, 5],
> >                   s.pH.std.01             = Xm[, 6],
> >                   s.calcium.std.01        = Xm[, 7],
> >                   s.carbon.std.01         = Xm[, 8],
> >                   s.water.std.01          = Xm[, 9],
> >                   mean.ndvi.std.01        = Xm[, 10])
> >
> > # And this is the stack for the ZAP model
> > StackPos.mesh1 <- inla.stack(
> >   tag  = "FitPos",
> >   data = list(AllY = cbind(UG4$SpeciesPos, NA)),

messages.subject: Reproducibility for INLA fitted value
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I realize that set.seed() doesn't work as expect when I fit a model with INLA, for example:

set.seed(1)
fit0<-inla(n ~ 1 +offset(log(popsize))+f(ID.NIS, model = "besag",graph=W2),
                 data = data.spa,
                 family = "poisson",
                 control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                 control.compute = list(dic = TRUE,waic=TRUE))

Then, I need to take fit0$summary.fitted.values$mean for further analysis with random forest. But each time I re-run the model, the fitted values slighly change and even thought the difference is extremely small, it leads to slightly different variable importance plot from random forest (I have set seed for random forest).

Is there any way we can deal with seed in INLA to make results reproducible?

Many thanks in advance.

Best regards,
Hanh.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Reproducibility for INLA fitted value
messages.body_plain:
The R random seed is essentially irrelevant for regular inla() runs, as it doesn't do MCMC. The differences you see are most likely due to numerical fluctuations due to order of operations in the parallel computations.
Normally, these fluctuations are negligible, but it means that, as nearly always when floating point computations are involved, and doubly when parallel computations are involved, exact equality should be expected.

For debugging purposes, you can use num.threads="1:1" to force single-threaded calculations, which normally does produce the exact same values each time, but for "production use", it's better to handle the floating point values appropriately instead (i.e., to not expect them to be exactly equal).

Finn

messages.subject: Understanding posterior marginals
messages.body_plain:
Hi group,

I'm very new to INLA and have been running test models on data subsets and am now trying to understand how to interpret spatial patterns in my outcome, which is a count modelled with the Poisson family. From going through the various books and tutorials, I understand that to do this it is better to summarize from model$marginals.random$id.num rather than model$summary.random$id.num, but I don't understand why. I guess my confusion is that I don't understand what the marginals represent. Why can't the median of each element of model$marginals.random$id.num or model$summary.random$id.num$`0.5quant` be exponentiated to estimate the effect size for each individual spatial unit, and why does inla.emarginal(exp, marginals) gives such a different value?

I hope my question is clear! My code is below, if it helps.

Thank you in advance for your insight on this!
Pascale

> formula = culex_tarsalis_females ~ trap_type + f(id.num, model="bym", graph=sayo_w30_y2016.graph, scale.model=T)
> model = inla(formula,
+              family="poisson",
+              offset=log(trap_nights_total),
+              data=abun_over,
+              control.predictor=list(compute=T, link=1),
+              control.compute=list(dic=T, cpo=T, waic=T))

zeta = lapply(model$marginals.random$id.num[1:Nareas], function(x) inla.emarginal(exp, x))
zeta2 = data.frame(id.num=seq(1, Nareas, 1), zeta = unlist(zeta))

> # from inla.emarginal()
> summary(zeta2$zeta)
Min.     1st Qu.   Median   Mean     3rd Qu.  Max.
0.02315  0.056459  1.69461  6.04676  5.68828  133.16567

> # from summary.random
> summary(exp(model$summary.random$id.num$`0.5quant`[1:Nareas]))
Min.     1st Qu.   Median   Mean      3rd Qu.   Max.
0.02013  0.31599   0.82253  3.27497   2.74362   97.51027

..summary  provide summaries for each marginals like E() STDEV()

only quantiles (and not expected values) survive a monotone

messages.body_plain:
yes, in general they are different

> r=inla(y ~ 1, data=data.frame(y=1), family="poisson")
> exp(r$summary.fixed[,"0.5quant"])
[1] 1.112208955
> inla.emarginal(exp, r$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
[1] 1.518630038

you can also transform the density from 'x' to 'exp(x)' and then take
the median

> exp.intercept = inla.tmarginal(exp, r$marginals.fixed$'(Intercept)')
> inla.qmarginal(0.5, exp.intercept)
[1] 1.109500839

the difference in the result compared to 1.1122.... is due to a finite
representation of the marginal internally

messages.subject: Error using two natural splines in one formula
messages.subject_clean: Error using two natural splines in one formula
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Is there a way around a fault I'm getting when using two natural splines, via the ns function. Here's a toy example:

require(splines) ; require(INLA)
set.seed(12344)
x=rnorm(100)
y=rnorm(100)
z=rnorm(100)
data=data.frame(x=x,y=y,z=z)
fml = y ~ ns(x) + ns(z)
mod = inla(formula = fml,data=data)

When this runs, I get:

 *** Key [1] is used twice and that is not allowed.
 *** A typical example where this happens is: y ~ x + f(x)
 *** Change this formula into: y ~ x + f(x2)
 *** where you define x2=x

it seems to be something to do with the way that the subset of each spline is fed into the INLA formula, but am currently unsure how to fix it.

Any help would be very welcome.

Thanks a lot.

Robbie

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Error using two natural splines in one formula
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Error using two natural splines in one formula
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
frequentist use of splines and Bayesian latent Gaussian models are never exactly equivalent since one refers to a maximum likelihood estimator and the other refers to a stochastic process model. However, ordinary cubic spline estimates are "equivalent" to the rw2 process model in the sense that for a rw2 process observed with additive independent gaussian noise, the posterior mode is the same the minimiser of a least squares problem with a cubic spline penalty, since the cubic spline minimises the same energy functional; the integral of the square of the second order derivative.
Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] R-INLA Man Page
messages.body_plain:
The package uses a somewhat hybrid documentation method for .Rd files, but the manual.pdf can be generated from those; it has nothing to do with CRAN.
Many of the .Rd files are nowadays generated via roxygen2, but some are generated by a bespoke system (since the package was started before roxygen2 was usable for this).
You can download/clone the github repository where all .Rd files are, and run devtools::build_manual().

But inla also has separate documentation for the latent models and priors, that live in separate, non-.Rd files (semi-automatically generated via latex, I think) that are normally opened via inla.doc(). Those aren't joined in a big document, but you could do that with a pdfjoin command or similar; should be possible in principle to auto-generate those documents to .Rd format as well, but it would take some effort; likely a bit easier to autogenerate a "models" document in RMarkdown format, but still would take effort to do.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] seasonal for diel
messages.body_plain:
That depends on the type of seasonality you're looking for.
The "seasonal" model is defined in inla.doc("seasonal"), but it wouldn't be my first choice for a _smooth_ seasonal model, especially not if you don't have regular data in time.
For that, I'd use a cyclic rw2 model instead, and yes, you can have a separate model component that models the daily cycle and one that models the annual cycle.
As a general advice, think about what type of model you think would be appropriate _first_, and then figure out how to implement that model with INLA (or a model close to that).

Finn

messages.subject: heteroskedasticity
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have been trying to work out how to fit the following model in INLA

Cover: response (percent cover ranging from 0 to 1)
Year: categorical predictor with 32 levels - ideally needs to be categoical for numerous reasons.
REEF_NAME: 'random effect' - approx 50 to 100 levels depending on the data location

BRMS
---------------
mod_brms.beta.disp <- brm(bf(Cover ~ Year + (1|REEF_NAME), phi~0+Year),
                                       data=dat,
                                       family=Beta(link='logit'),
                                       iter=1e4, warmup=5e3, thin=5,
                                       chains=4, cores=4,
                                       prior = prior(normal(0, 3), class = "b") +
                                           prior(normal(0, 3), class = "Intercept") +
                                           prior(gamma(2, 1), class = "sd")
                                       )

glmmTMB
--------------------
mod_glmmTMB.beta.disp <- glmmTMB(Cover ~ Year + (1|REEF_NAME),
                                     dispformula = ~Year,
                                     data=dat,
                                     family=beta_family())

Whilst these two models run find, the stan model in particular takes about 11 hours to run.

The following INLA model runs in about 30 seconds and yields results indistinguishable from brms (without phii ~..) and glmmTMB (without disp ~ ..):
mod_inla.beta <-inla(Cover~Year + f(REEF_NAME, model='iid'),
                                                    dat=dat,
                                                    family='beta',
                                                    control.fixed=list(mean=0, prec=0.001,
                                                    mean.intercept=0.5, prec.intercept=0.001)
)

Kind regards and thanks in advance

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] heteroskedasticity
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,

you didn't define the heteroscedasticity in the text, so it took me a while to realise that the brms and glmmmTB code has some extra features.
It looks like you want the variance of the REEF_NAME variables to be different for each Year?

>From what I can tell in your model construction, that means that you could just estimate a completely separate model for each year, since there's nothing to link them together.
Unless you want another hierarchical layer for the variances? I don't believe that's possible in the R-INLA implementation, since it doesn't follow the theta->latent->observed hierarchical structure.

However, this extra structure can in principle be approximated using a non-linear predictor in the inlabru package. By parameterising the variances as transformations of N(0,1) variables, one can construct a non-linear model via

  comp <- ~ Year + REEF(REEF_NAME, model = "iid") + scale(Year, model = "iid", hyper = list(prec=list(initial=0,fixed=TRUE)), constr=TRUE)
  formula <- Cover ~ Year + REEF * scalequantile(pnorm(scale))
  bru(comp, like(data=dat, formula=formula, family="beta"), options=list(control.inla=..., ...))

where scalequantile() is the quantile function for the desired prior for the scaling parameters. The resulting variances would be determined by the combination of a precision hyperparameter for the REEF random effects and the Year-wise scaling parameters. The sum-to-zero constraint is to ensure identifiability, but there are other options, such as fixing the precision of REEF instead, in which scalequantile() would directly determine the standard deviation priors, but that would then be indistinguishable from estimating separate models for each Year.  The suggestion above will estimate a common precision parameter, and the scale parameters model the deviation from that overall precision.

If you use this approach, please contact me off list as well, as I'm not aware of this feature being used for this particular purpose yet.

PS. "scalequantile(pnorm())" should ideally be implemented as a single function that used log.p=TRUE and lower.tail=TRUE/FALSE intelligently to preserve as much numerical precision as possible. I'm planning an automated feature for that in the package soon(ish) as we're finding more and more uses for this technique.

Finn

beta. some, or rather, a few, likelihood models have that option, but

if you know the scaling of the precisions there is the argument 'scale',

On Thu, 2021-05-20 at 01:11 +0100, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> Hi Murray,
>
> you didn't define the heteroscedasticity in the text, so it took me a
> while to realise that the brms and glmmmTB code has some extra
> features.
> It looks like you want the variance of the REEF_NAME variables to be
> different for each Year?
>
> From what I can tell in your model construction, that means that you
> could just estimate a completely separate model for each year, since
> there's nothing to link them together.
> Unless you want another hierarchical layer for the variances? I don't
> believe that's possible in the R-INLA implementation, since it doesn't
> follow the theta->latent->observed hierarchical structure.
>
> However, this extra structure can in principle be approximated using a
> non-linear predictor in the inlabru package. By parameterising the
> variances as transformations of N(0,1) variables, one can construct a
> non-linear model via
>
>   comp <- ~ Year + REEF(REEF_NAME, model = "iid") + scale(Year, model
> = "iid", hyper = list(prec=list(initial=0,fixed=TRUE)), constr=TRUE)
>   formula <- Cover ~ Year + REEF * scalequantile(pnorm(scale))
>   bru(comp, like(data=dat, formula=formula, family="beta"),
> options=list(control.inla=..., ...))
>
> where scalequantile() is the quantile function for the desired prior
> for the scaling parameters. The resulting variances would be
> determined by the combination of a precision hyperparameter for the
> REEF random effects and the Year-wise scaling parameters. The sum-to-
> zero constraint is to ensure identifiability, but there are other
> options, such as fixing the precision of REEF instead, in which
> scalequantile() would directly determine the standard deviation
> priors, but that would then be indistinguishable from estimating
> separate models for each Year.  The suggestion above will estimate a
> common precision parameter, and the scale parameters model the
> deviation from that overall precision.
>
> If you use this approach, please contact me off list as well, as I'm
> not aware of this feature being used for this particular purpose yet.
>
> PS. "scalequantile(pnorm())" should ideally be implemented as a single
> function that used log.p=TRUE and lower.tail=TRUE/FALSE intelligently
> to preserve as much numerical precision as possible. I'm planning an
> automated feature for that in the package soon(ish) as we're finding
> more and more uses for this technique.
>
> Finn
>
> On Wed, 19 May 2021 at 23:24, Murray Logan <i.obe...@gmail.com>
> wrote:
> > Hi,
> >
> > I have been trying to work out how to fit the following model in
> > INLA
> >
> > Cover: response (percent cover ranging from 0 to 1)
> > Year: categorical predictor with 32 levels - ideally needs to be
> > categoical for numerous reasons.
> > REEF_NAME: 'random effect' - approx 50 to 100 levels depending on
> > the data location
> >
> > BRMS
> > ---------------
> > mod_brms.beta.disp <- brm(bf(Cover ~ Year + (1|REEF_NAME),
> > phi~0+Year),
> >                                        data=dat,
> >                                        family=Beta(link='logit'),
> >                                        iter=1e4, warmup=5e3, thin=5,
> >                                        chains=4, cores=4,
> >                                        prior = prior(normal(0, 3),
> > class = "b") +
> >                                            prior(normal(0, 3), class
> > = "Intercept") +
> >                                            prior(gamma(2, 1), class
> > = "sd")
> >                                        )
> >
> > glmmTMB
> > --------------------
> > mod_glmmTMB.beta.disp <- glmmTMB(Cover ~ Year + (1|REEF_NAME),
> >                                      dispformula = ~Year,
> >                                      data=dat,
> >                                      family=beta_family())
> >
> > Whilst these two models run find, the stan model in particular takes
> > about 11 hours to run.
> >
> > The following INLA model runs in about 30 seconds and yields results
> > indistinguishable from brms (without phii ~..) and glmmTMB (without
> > disp ~ ..):
> > mod_inla.beta <-inla(Cover~Year + f(REEF_NAME, model='iid'),
> >                                                     dat=dat,
> >                                                     family='beta',
> >
> > control.fixed=list(mean=0, prec=0.001,
> >
> > mean.intercept=0.5, prec.intercept=0.001)
> > )
> >
> >
> > Kind regards and thanks in advance

On Thursday, 20 May 2021 at 16:23:09 UTC+10 he...@r-inla.org wrote:
>
> its possible to allow for a linear model for the log precision for the
> beta. some, or rather, a few, likelihood models have that option, but
> not yet for family=beta. its about one day of work...
>
> if you know the scaling of the precisions there is the argument 'scale',
> but this what you want to estimate, not set.
>
>
> On Thu, 2021-05-20 at 01:11 +0100, Finn Lindgren wrote:
> > Hi Murray,
> >
> > you didn't define the heteroscedasticity in the text, so it took me a
> > while to realise that the brms and glmmmTB code has some extra
> > features.
> > It looks like you want the variance of the REEF_NAME variables to be
> > different for each Year?
> >
> > From what I can tell in your model construction, that means that you
> > could just estimate a completely separate model for each year, since
> > there's nothing to link them together.
> > Unless you want another hierarchical layer for the variances? I don't
> > believe that's possible in the R-INLA implementation, since it doesn't
> > follow the theta->latent->observed hierarchical structure.
> >
> > However, this extra structure can in principle be approximated using a
> > non-linear predictor in the inlabru package. By parameterising the
> > variances as transformations of N(0,1) variables, one can construct a
> > non-linear model via
> >
> >   comp <- ~ Year + REEF(REEF_NAME, model = "iid") + scale(Year, model
> > = "iid", hyper = list(prec=list(initial=0,fixed=TRUE)), constr=TRUE)
> >   formula <- Cover ~ Year + REEF * scalequantile(pnorm(scale))
> >   bru(comp, like(data=dat, formula=formula, family="beta"),
> > options=list(control.inla=..., ...))
> >
> > where scalequantile() is the quantile function for the desired prior
> > for the scaling parameters. The resulting variances would be
> > determined by the combination of a precision hyperparameter for the
> > REEF random effects and the Year-wise scaling parameters. The sum-to-
> > zero constraint is to ensure identifiability, but there are other
> > options, such as fixing the precision of REEF instead, in which
> > scalequantile() would directly determine the standard deviation
> > priors, but that would then be indistinguishable from estimating
> > separate models for each Year.  The suggestion above will estimate a
> > common precision parameter, and the scale parameters model the
> > deviation from that overall precision.
> >
> > If you use this approach, please contact me off list as well, as I'm
> > not aware of this feature being used for this particular purpose yet.
> >
> > PS. "scalequantile(pnorm())" should ideally be implemented as a single
> > function that used log.p=TRUE and lower.tail=TRUE/FALSE intelligently
> > to preserve as much numerical precision as possible. I'm planning an
> > automated feature for that in the package soon(ish) as we're finding
> > more and more uses for this technique.
> >
> > Finn
> >
> > On Wed, 19 May 2021 at 23:24, Murray Logan <i.obe...@gmail.com>
> > wrote:
> > > Hi,
> > >
> > > I have been trying to work out how to fit the following model in
> > > INLA
> > >
> > > Cover: response (percent cover ranging from 0 to 1)
> > > Year: categorical predictor with 32 levels - ideally needs to be
> > > categoical for numerous reasons.
> > > REEF_NAME: 'random effect' - approx 50 to 100 levels depending on
> > > the data location
> > >
> > > BRMS
> > > ---------------
> > > mod_brms.beta.disp <- brm(bf(Cover ~ Year + (1|REEF_NAME),
> > > phi~0+Year),
> > >                                        data=dat,
> > >                                        family=Beta(link='logit'),
> > >                                        iter=1e4, warmup=5e3, thin=5,
> > >                                        chains=4, cores=4,
> > >                                        prior = prior(normal(0, 3),
> > > class = "b") +
> > >                                            prior(normal(0, 3), class
> > > = "Intercept") +
> > >                                            prior(gamma(2, 1), class
> > > = "sd")
> > >                                        )
> > >
> > > glmmTMB
> > > --------------------
> > > mod_glmmTMB.beta.disp <- glmmTMB(Cover ~ Year + (1|REEF_NAME),
> > >                                      dispformula = ~Year,
> > >                                      data=dat,
> > >                                      family=beta_family())
> > >
> > > Whilst these two models run find, the stan model in particular takes
> > > about 11 hours to run.
> > >
> > > The following INLA model runs in about 30 seconds and yields results
> > > indistinguishable from brms (without phii ~..) and glmmTMB (without
> > > disp ~ ..):
> > > mod_inla.beta <-inla(Cover~Year + f(REEF_NAME, model='iid'),
> > >                                                     dat=dat,
> > >                                                     family='beta',
> > >
> > > control.fixed=list(mean=0, prec=0.001,
> > >
> > > mean.intercept=0.5, prec.intercept=0.001)
> > > )
> > >
> > >
> > > Kind regards and thanks in advance

messages.subject: Species richness predictions: advice needed on approach
messages.subject_clean: Species richness predictions: advice needed on approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I’d like to invite suggestions on how to approach a piece of research. I’m trying to predict areas of higher vs. lower plant biodiversity across the island of New Guinea, on the basis of geographically very biased collection records. Having constructed various cost-distance rasters, it’s easy to see that collection is heavily skewed towards areas accessible from towns and roads. Also, a lot of older records are vaguely georeferenced. I had a couple of ideas:

1. Count the number of unique species recorded in 25x25km grids across the island, use poly2nb to construct a lattice from the grid, and build a formula for number of species ~ PCA components of environmental variables, plus the cost-distance raster, plus a spatial term as follows:

f(ID, model = "bym", graph = Lattice.adj, scale.model = TRUE,

    hyper = list(prec.unstruct = list(prior = "loggamma", param = c(1,0.001)),

      prec.spatial =  list(prior = "loggamma", param = c(1,0.001)))

...although perhaps the cost-distance element is part of what the spatial term estimates, and hence unnecessary?

This would look a bit like a joint Species Distribution Model, although without estimating any individual species’ ranges – but we have very sparse records anyway, since people tend to record novelties and ignore common species, and I’ve had little luck with JSDMs or ensemble SDMs.

2. Since the grids are arbitrary and I have a lot of data georeferenced to within 1km, I thought maybe an inlabru mesh approach would work, with the density of records as a proxy for biodiversity once the spatial effecgt of recording effort had been accounted for, e.g.:

mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(loc=speciesRecords, boundary=NGboundary, max.edge = c(25, 250), cutoff = 3,

                      crs="+proj=utm +zone=54 +south +ellps=WGS72 +units=km +no_defs")

matern <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,

                               prior.sigma = c(1, 0.01), prior.range = c(25, 0.01))

comp <- coordinates ~

  costpath(speciesRecords$costpath, model = "linear") + # from the cost-distance raster

[....then various PCA components...] +

  mySmooth(coordinates, model = matern) + Intercept(1)

fit <- lgcp(comp, speciesRecords, samplers = NGboundary, domain = list(coordinates = mesh))

As an INLA novice I’ve been following online advice rather blindly so not even sure if the spatial modelling terms are appropriate.

In particular:

- Is there any way of separating out the spatial effect of certain areas being hard to reach, from the ‘normal’ spatial autocorrelation?

- How could I incorporate estimates of collection record coordinate uncertainty?

- Is there any way of extracting a ‘spatial field’ effect I could feed into SDM models as though it were another environmental variable?

Please do ask for more info / clarification – I don’t want to ramble on though.

Best wishes,

Michael

messages.subject: Spatial Gradient for the latent Gaussian field through SPDE
messages.subject_clean: Spatial Gradient for the latent Gaussian field through SPDE
messages.body_plain:
HI everyone,

I am new to INLA as well as the SPDE approach for latent Gaussian field. I am currently interested in obtaining a spatial gradient/Hessian estimates of the posterior intensity field obtained from a LGCP model after using the SPDE approach.

My understanding is that there is restriction on the differentiability of the latent field given the smoothness parameter  for the Matern covariance function. Nevertheless, assume that my Matern field is differentiable (or maybe even twice differentiable) in the spatial coordinates, is there some kind of simple way of obtaining an estimates for the gradients and Hessian after getting the solution from the SPDE approach?

My initial thought is that if the solution to the latent field is provided by a basis function expansion, it should be relatively easy to get the spatial gradient since we only need to differentiate the basis function with respect to the coordinates. But since the basis functions used in the SPDE approach is piecewise linear on the triangle mesh, won't there be locations in the field that are not differentiable? For example, points on the edge of two triangle. This seems to contradict the original assumption that the Matern field is differentiable, although my understanding here could be incorrect.

My main question here is that by using a piecewise linear function, can we simply get a gradient estimates of the latent field? If so, how should I do it in INLA? If not, will there be any development in the code to implement gradient estimates of the latent field?

Thank you very much!

Best,
David

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Spatial Gradient for the latent Gaussian field through SPDE
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial Gradient for the latent Gaussian field through SPDE
messages.body_plain:
The inla.spde2.matern and inla.spde.pcmatern implementations are limited to operator order alpha=2 which in dimension 2 only gives one mean square derivative of the field, so the Hessian is not well defined. The gradient of the finite element representation is piecewise constant, so it does give an approximation of the gradient at least; it's an approximation that's good for spatial integrals of the gradient (by the finite element construction) but less good for pointwise values.  The `inla.fmesher.smorg` function has a parameter `gradients` for allowing the construction of the weighting matrices dx, dy, and dz, for derivatives in different directions (For a planar mesh, dx %*% field gives x-derivatives for the whole field).

For higher order derivatives, you need a field with larger alpha value (easiest to implement via inla.rgeneric) and higher order basis functions, which is possible but not implemented in the R-INLA package.
Recall that for alpha = 2, the SPDE operator is (kappa^2 - Hessian) x(s) ds = dW(s), so the Hessian of the field is as non-continuous as spatial white noise (smoothness -1, i.e. less than continuous ), so even though one can compute an approximation in distribution sense (i.e. that has sensible properties when integrated over space, via a rescaling of the G1 matrix) the continuous interpretation doesn't have pointwise meaning.

Finn

Finn

messages.subject: Reproducibility of Knorr-Held spatiotemporal models
messages.body_plain:
I was experimenting with the Knorr-Held
spacetime models, as shown in Ch 7.1 of
Blangiardo+Cameletti. I was a bit surprised to
see that while the Type-I and Type-IV results
reproduced exactly (at least as they are reported
by INLA's summary function), the Type-II and
Type-III did not; and this persisted even after
setting the random seed before running the models.
The differences between runs can be quite substantial.

Should I be concerned about this? Is there something about
the Type-II and Type-III models that would lead one
to expect this behavior, when the Type-I and Type-IV
models don't show it?

I'm running INLA version 20.03.17 on MS Windows-10 (64-bit).

Here's the script, mostly truncated from the
version supplied by Blangiardo + Cameletti

### R code for Chapter 7.1 - Georgia Data
# This does the 4 types of space-time interactions a la Knorr-Held
### Last update: 18/08/2014

# modified by pav for working directory and other folders

# This version just does the Type I-IV models, without any
# intervening stuff or graphics

###################################################
### Set working directory and load packages
###################################################
#remove(list=ls())
my.dir <- "c:/work/R/blangiardo/"

require(INLA)
inla.setOption(scale.model.default=FALSE)

set.seed(12345)

require(maptools)

###################################################
### Code for Section 7.1.1
###################################################

data <- read.csv(paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/data.final.csv",sep=""))
georgia <- readShapePoly(paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/co13_d00.shp",sep=""))

# Remove duplicates (area 88 and 94)
names <- georgia$NAME
georgia <- georgia[-c(99,100,105,137),]
data.georgia <- attr(georgia, "data")

low.vector <- as.vector(as.matrix(data[,2:12])) #by column
E.vector <- as.vector(as.matrix(data[,13:23]))  #by column
year <- numeric(0)
for(i in 1:11){
  year<- append(year,rep(i,dim(data)[1]))
}

# county replicates the county names 11 times
county <- as.factor(rep(data[,1],11))

data <- data.frame(y= low.vector, E= E.vector, ID.area=as.numeric(county), ID.area1=as.numeric(county), year=year,
                   ID.year = year, ID.year1=year, ID.area.year = seq(1,length(county)))

# Spatial graph
Georgia.adj <- paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/Georgia.graph",sep="")
# Temporal graph
Temp.adj <- paste(my.dir,"LBWGeorgiaData/Temp.graph",sep="")

data$ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int> <- data$ID.area # PAV I've added these to data
data$ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int> <- data$ID.year

###################################################
#--- Type I interaction ---#
formula.intI<- y ~ + f(ID.area,model="bym", graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") + f(ID.year1,model="iid") + f(ID.area.year,model="iid")

mod.intI <- inla(formula.intI,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                 control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

summary(mod.intI)

#--- Type II interaction ---#
formula.intII<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") + f(ID.year1,model="iid") +
  f(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,model="iid", group=ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,control.group=list(model="rw2"))

mod.intII <- inla(formula.intII,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

summary(mod.intII)

#--- Type III interaction ---#
formula.intIII<- y ~  f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") +
  f(ID.year1,model="iid") +
  f(ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,model="iid", group=ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,control.group=list(model="besag", graph=Georgia.adj))

mod.intIII <- inla(formula.intIII,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                   control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                   control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

summary(mod.intIII)

#--- Type IV interaction ---#
formula.intIV<- y ~ f(ID.area,model="bym",graph=Georgia.adj) +
  f(ID.year,model="rw2") +
  f(ID.year1,model="iid") +
  f(ID.area.int <http://ID.area.int>,model="besag", graph=Georgia.adj,group=ID.year.int <http://ID.year.int>,control.group=list(model="rw2"))

mod.intIV <- inla(formula.intIV,family="poisson",data=data,E=E,
                  control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
                  control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE))

summary(mod.intIV)

messages.subject: Binomial spatiotemporal model
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA –
team,

 I am trying
to run a binomial spatiotemporal model including 6 covariates and 18 years. It
comprises 16651 observations (this corresponds to 70% of the data for training
purposes). The number of presences and absences per year is balanced. It took
approximately 9 hours to compile and in the end, it showed that the values of
DIC are Inf. I tried in another cluster, this time with Pardiso, and it took
some minutes but the model crashed. I would like to have suggestions about how
I can handle this issue.

 Here is the
code:

library (INLA)

library (dplyr)

inla.setOption(pardiso.license =
"./Data/pardisovub.lic")

library(raster) # for working with rasters

library(maps) # additional helpful mapping packages

source('./Data/spde-book-functions.R')

# 1. Input data #

data = read.csv(file = 'datasortplus_summer.csv')

data_1<-data%>%dplyr::select(Year,Lon_M,Lat_M,MUN,ANC,DC,SST,SALI,GSST,
BAT,CHL)

scale2 <- function(x, na.rm = FALSE) (x - mean(x,
na.rm = na.rm)) / sd(x, na.rm)

# 2. Standardise covariates

data_1 = data_1 %>%
mutate_at(c('DC','SST','SALI','GSST','BAT','CHL'),scale2)

data_1 = na.omit(data_1)

data_1$MUN<-ifelse(data_1$MUN>0,1,0)

RNGkind(sample.kind = 'Rounding')

set.seed(1234)

sample_size = floor(0.7*nrow(data_1))

samplet<- sample(seq_len(nrow(data_1)),size =
sample_size)

data_1t<-data_1[samplet,]

data_1p<-data_1[-samplet,]

data_1t<-data_1t[order(data_1t$Year),]#important to
reorder

x_loc = cbind(data_1t$Lon_M, data_1t$Lat_M)

spdat <- data_1t

coordinates(spdat) <- ~ Lon_M + Lat_M

proj4string(spdat) <- "+init=epsg:4326"

kmproj <- CRS("+proj=utm +zone=18S ellps=WGS84
+units=km")

# Project data

x_loc_utm <- spTransform(spdat, kmproj)

# 3. mesh

mesh = readRDS('mesh_summer_plus.rds')

#3.1 Build the spde

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,

                            prior.range = c(50,
0.01),

                            prior.sigma = c(5,
0.3))

# 4. Spatiotemporal model

t<-18

mesh.t1 = inla.mesh.1d(1:18)

data_1t$Year<-as.numeric(factor(data_1t$Year))

# 4.1 Projector matrix

Aspte<- inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh,
loc=x_loc_utm,group.mesh =mesh.t1, group = data_1t$Year)

# 4.2 Stack data

Xm = model.matrix(~ -1 + DC + SST + SALI + GSST + BAT
+ CHL, data = data_1t)

N = nrow(data_1t)

X = data.frame(Intercept = rep(1,N), DC=Xm[,1],
SST=Xm[,2], SALI=Xm[,3], GSST=Xm[,4], BAT=Xm[,5],CHL=Xm[,6])

index.st <http://index.st> <- inla.spde.make.index('i', n.spde =
mesh$n, n.group = 18)

# 4.3 Index spatiotemporal

stk.dat.st <http://stk.dat.st> <- inla.stack(tag='dat', data = list(z =
data_1t$MUN),

                         A = list(Aspte,1),
effects = list(index.st <http://index.st>,X))

# 4.4 Formula

f.DCst <- z ~ -1 + Intercept + DC + SST + SALI +
GSST + BAT + CHL +f(i, model = spde,
group = i.group, control.group = list(model = 'ar1',

hyper=list(theta=list(prior='pc.cor1', param=c(0,
0.9)))))

# 5. Fitting the model

r.DCst <- inla(f.DCst, family = 'binomial',

control.family=list(link='logit'),

data = inla.stack.data(stk.dat.st <http://stk.dat.st>),

               control.compute
= list(waic=TRUE,dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE,openmp.strategy='huge'),  control.predictor = list(A =
inla.stack.A(stk.dat.st <http://stk.dat.st>), link = 1, compute=TRUE), control.inla = list(strategy
= 'adaptive', int.strategy = 'eb',verbose=TRUE)

saveRDS(r.DCst,'r.DCst.rds')

And I am
attaching a picture of the mesh with 1664 vertices.

Thank you
for your time,

Noelia

messages.subject: Calibrating overfitting SPDE model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Some background:
I will preface this by saying that I am still fairly new to INLA.
I have been working on specifying a SPDE model, to analyse factors explaining per-pixel rates of a degradation index, in a pre-defined study region (approx. 350km x 170km). Based on yearly degradation maps, I calculated the overall pixel rate, and built a model with Gaussian family,  specifying priors with 'inla.spde2.pcmatern' (see code below).

The problem:
Looking at plots of the random field compared to the model predictions, the two are essentially indistinguishable, suggesting the random effect is taking over (I think).
I did some posterior predictive model checking, and the model seemed to be overfitting quite drastically:

Interestingly, when I checked the model using cross-validation based on CPO and PIT, the histogram appears to show a rather uniform distribution:

Tried so far:
Following advice in this thread <https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/ZhZVu8YPI8I>, I added a local dispersion effect, as iid effect in linear predictor. The result seems to be that the histogram of the posterior predictive p-values is essentially flipped:

The cross validation histogram looks very similar to the previous one:

I tried setting the alpha parameter to 2/3, as suggested in the same threat, but to no avail.

Questions:
Was the model specified correctly, to begin with?
If the model is correct, what could I attempt next to calibrate the model for a better fit?
Any help is greatly appreciated!

Joris

The code (my apologies, not sure how to format this as code):
-----------------------------------------------------------------------
deg500 <- a raster stack, containing 20 rasters with 500m pixel resolution
load("BG_raw_spdf.RData"))   a SpatialPointsDataFrame, containing the covariates
annRain <- yearly rainfall for the time period
studyArea <- shapefile for the study area

### ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
time <- 1:nlayers(deg500)
# Compute the overall slope of degradation, accounting for rainfall in a given year
slowfun <- function(y) {
      if(all(is.na <http://is.na>(y))){
            NA
      } else {
            m = lm(y ~ time + annRain$mean); summary(m)$coefficients[2]   # get time
      }
}

deg500_rate <- calc(deg500, slowfun)

### Basic INLA model predicting rate from various covariates:
### ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

## Add the rate to the raw_spdf:
deg500_rate_spdf <- as(deg500_rate, "SpatialPointsDataFrame")
deg500_rate_spdf <- deg500_rate_spdf[!is.na <http://is.na>(deg500_rate_spdf@data$layer), ]

xy_raw  <- apply(round(coordinates(raw_spdf), 6), 1, paste, collapse = "_")
xy_rate <- apply(round(coordinates(deg500_rate_spdf), 6), 1, paste, collapse = "_")

raw_spdf <- raw_spdf[order(xy_raw), ]
deg500_rate_spdf <- deg500_rate_spdf[xy_rate %in% xy_raw, ]
deg500_rate_spdf <- deg500_rate_spdf[order(xy_rate[xy_rate %in% xy_raw]), ]
raw_spdf$deg_rate <- deg500_rate_spdf$layer * 10  # Small decimal numbers will use more memory to get to integer. Also easier to read, adn index is arbitrary anyways

## Transform and scale covariates:
raw_spdf$lpop <- log(raw_spdf$pop + 1)  # log(x+1) for right skewed data containing zeros
raw_spdf$ltlu <- log(raw_spdf$tlu + 1)
raw_spdf$pop_s <- c(scale(raw_spdf$lpop))
raw_spdf$rain_s <- c(scale(raw_spdf$rain))
raw_spdf$tlu_s <- c(scale(raw_spdf$ltlu))

## Make a mesh:
max.edge = diff(range(raw_spdf@coords[, 2]))/15

bound.outer = diff(range(raw_spdf@coords[, 2]))/3
mesh <- inla.mesh.2d(
      boundary = studyArea,
      loc = coordinates(raw_spdf),
      max.edge = c(1,5)*max.edge,  # For filling in area
      cutoff = max.edge/5,
      offset = c(max.edge, bound.outer),    # Expanding outside actual locations. Determine inner and outer offset
)
# and the spde:
A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh, loc=data.matrix(coordinates(raw_spdf)))  # Combine actual points with mesh

# covariates:
Xcov = data.frame(intercept=1,
                  pop_s = raw_spdf$pop_s,
                  rain_s = raw_spdf$rain_s,
                  tlu_s = raw_spdf$tlu_s,
                  CA1 = (raw_spdf$CA == 1) * 1,  # CCRO
                  CA2 = (raw_spdf$CA == 2) * 1,  # NP
                  CA3 = (raw_spdf$CA == 3) * 1)  # WMA

Xcov = as.matrix(Xcov)
colnames(Xcov)
stck <- inla.stack(tag='est',     # stack is INLA data structure
                   data=list(deg_rate=raw_spdf$deg_rate),
                   effects=list(
                         s=1:mesh$n,     # spatial random effect
                         iidx=1:nrow(raw_spdf),  # iid random effect
                         Xcov=Xcov),
                   A = list(A, 1, 1)

## define the model:
# - sd(raw_spdf@coords[, 2])/10
# - 0.5*diff(range(raw_spdf@coords[, 2]))

spde = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh,
                           alpha = 3/2,
                           prior.range = c(1.6, 0.5),
                           prior.sigma = c(0.08, 0.1))

hyper.iid = list(prec = list(prior = 'pc.prec', param = c(0.08, 0.1)))

formula = deg_rate ~ -1 + Xcov +
      f(s, model=spde)  +               # spatial random effect
      f(iidx, model="iid", hyper=hyper.iid)   # iid random effect

## make some linear combinations, for effect plots:
pop_lc <- inla.make.lincombs(Xcov1 = rep(1, 100),
                             Xcov2 = seq(min(raw_spdf$pop_s), max(raw_spdf$pop_s), len = 100))
names(pop_lc) <- paste0("pop", 1:100)
rain_lc <- inla.make.lincombs(Xcov1 = rep(1, 100),
                              Xcov3 = seq(min(raw_spdf$rain_s), max(raw_spdf$rain_s), len = 100))
names(rain_lc) <- paste0("rain", 1:100)
tlu_lc <- inla.make.lincombs(Xcov1 = rep(1, 100),
                             Xcov4 = seq(min(raw_spdf$tlu_s), max(raw_spdf$tlu_s), len = 100))
names(tlu_lc) <- paste0("tlu", 1:100)

      geom_point(data = mapdata, aes(x=x, y=y, col = predicted)) +
      coord_equal() +
      theme_minimal()

      geom_point(data = mapdata, aes(x=x, y=y, col = pred_sd), cex = 0.5) +
      coord_equal() +
      theme_minimal()

      geom_polygon(data = studyArea, aes(long, lat, group = group), fill = NA, col = 'black') +
      coord_equal()

messages.body_plain:
Hi Joris,

the "add an idd effect" from the other thread really only makes sense when the observation likelihood isn't already an iid Gaussian additive effect. E.g., if the observation model is Poisson, then adding an iid effect to the predictor acts as an overdispersion effect.

But in your case with Gaussian observations, we can see that the estimation simply redistributes the variance ~ 1/20 into two ~ 1/40 variances (though the clear way in which it does that _is_ a surprise to me!), leading to effectively the same model, and it's just where the observation noise is entered into the model that is adjusted.

This leads me to believe that the problem lies in the INLAutils::ggplot_inla_residuals() function itself, and that what it computes isn't as well defined a quantity as it should be; You may need to dig into the code for that package to see what they actually compute, and what mathematical object that is. The documentation doesn't say, so I would be inclined not to use that function until I figured out if it actually computes/plots something sensible.

It appears to me it's plotting the "linear predictor" posterior probabilities computed for the observed values, but that doesn't include the observation model itself, so it isn't the correct posterior probabilities of predictive distributions, since those need to involve the observation model as well. This is done correctly for the CPO calculations, which is likely why those consistently look ok!
Pet peeve: this misconception seems common in frequentist-to-bayesian text that incorrectly transpose point estimation methods as if they can be applied without modification to posterior distributions, which is incorrect!

Finn

TL/DR: it seems ggplot_inla_residuals uses the posterior predictive distribution for the linear predictor instead of the posterior predictive distribution for the observations.

Except for the CPO/PIT calculations from inla() itself, the latter typically needs inla.posterior.sample() to compute/estimate properly.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Yes, the only difference between linear.predictor and fitted.values is that fitted.values applies the (inverse of the) link function (which is the identity in your case), so it doesn't include the observation distribution part of posterior predictions.
CPO does include all the needed parts, so is the appropriate part to look at for this type of posterior check. But the observed vs point prediction scatter plot can also be useful; in your case it illustrates the slight shrinkage of the estimated model towards a flat field (since the scatter plot isn't centered around the 1-1 correspondence) which can either be ok, or an indication of oversmoothing (i.e. the opposite to overfitting!!!).
Further calculations of this type are only needed for fully out-of-sample predictions (In some models, the leave-one-out cross-validation that CPO involves isn't the appropriate tool to use.)

I would start by plotting the results spatially. You can also do a spatial plot of the observed-"point prediction" to check for spatial patterns in that, etc.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Calibrating overfitting SPDE model
messages.body_plain:
Excellent, thank you once again for your detailed explanation and input!

On Wednesday, 26 May 2021 at 15:54:07 UTC+1 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> Yes, the only difference between linear.predictor and fitted.values is that fitted.values applies the (inverse of the) link function (which is the identity in your case), so it doesn't include the observation distribution part of posterior predictions.
> CPO does include all the needed parts, so is the appropriate part to look at for this type of posterior check. But the observed vs point prediction scatter plot can also be useful; in your case it illustrates the slight shrinkage of the estimated model towards a flat field (since the scatter plot isn't centered around the 1-1 correspondence) which can either be ok, or an indication of oversmoothing (i.e. the opposite to overfitting!!!).
> Further calculations of this type are only needed for fully out-of-sample predictions (In some models, the leave-one-out cross-validation that CPO involves isn't the appropriate tool to use.)
>
> I would start by plotting the results spatially. You can also do a spatial plot of the observed-"point prediction" to check for spatial patterns in that, etc.
>
> Finn
>
> On Wed, 26 May 2021 at 15:44, 'Joris Wiethase' via R-inla discussion group <r-inla-disc...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> > Hi Finn,
> >
> > thank you for your input, it is very much appreciated! Good to know that including the iid effect doesn't makes sense (shows how little I know about the subject matter!).
> > In the Wang et al. (2018) book ("Bayesian Regression Modeling with INLA"), I have come across some code that produces the same plot; I suspect that is the code underlying the  INLAutils::ggplot_inla_residuals() function:
> >
> > predicted.p.value <- c()
> > n <- length(raw_spdf[, 1])
> > for(i in (1:n)) {
> >   predicted.p.value[i] <- inla.pmarginal(q = raw_spdf$deg_rate[i],
> >                                          marginal=res$marginals.fitted.values[[i]])
> > }
> > hist(predicted.p.value,main="",xlab="Posterior predictive p-value")
> >
> >
> >
> > Considering the CPO plot is the one to trust, do I conclude that the model is specified and working correctly? Or are there other checks to be done first?
> >
> >
> >
> > On Wednesday, 26 May 2021 at 15:00:30 UTC+1 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > > TL/DR: it seems ggplot_inla_residuals uses the posterior predictive distribution for the linear predictor instead of the posterior predictive distribution for the observations.
> > >
> > > Except for the CPO/PIT calculations from inla() itself, the latter typically needs inla.posterior.sample() to compute/estimate properly.
> > >
> > > Finn
> > >
> > > On Wed, 26 May 2021 at 14:57, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > Hi Joris,
> > > >
> > > > the "add an idd effect" from the other thread really only makes sense when the observation likelihood isn't already an iid Gaussian additive effect. E.g., if the observation model is Poisson, then adding an iid effect to the predictor acts as an overdispersion effect.
> > > >
> > > > But in your case with Gaussian observations, we can see that the estimation simply redistributes the variance ~ 1/20 into two ~ 1/40 variances (though the clear way in which it does that _is_ a surprise to me!), leading to effectively the same model, and it's just where the observation noise is entered into the model that is adjusted.
> > > >
> > > > This leads me to believe that the problem lies in the INLAutils::ggplot_inla_residuals() function itself, and that what it computes isn't as well defined a quantity as it should be; You may need to dig into the code for that package to see what they actually compute, and what mathematical object that is. The documentation doesn't say, so I would be inclined not to use that function until I figured out if it actually computes/plots something sensible.
> > > >
> > > > It appears to me it's plotting the "linear predictor" posterior probabilities computed for the observed values, but that doesn't include the observation model itself, so it isn't the correct posterior probabilities of predictive distributions, since those need to involve the observation model as well. This is done correctly for the CPO calculations, which is likely why those consistently look ok!
> > > > Pet peeve: this misconception seems common in frequentist-to-bayesian text that incorrectly transpose point estimation methods as if they can be applied without modification to posterior distributions, which is incorrect!
> > > >
> > > > Finn
> > > >
> > > >

messages.subject_clean: Extremely high slope estimate for one covariate
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I was modeling on some bird data, and I found a extremely high slope estimate with my model, which looks like this:

Other slope estimates are about +-1, but the genome_heterozygosity is 20-40. I don't know what happened.

In the practice of modeling, each time I put one variate into the model, and the variate is added only if the wAIC decrease by 2 or more.

Besides, will it be a normalization or standerization problem?

My code:
```
#### reasonable values for mesh
minME<-10;maxME<-50;co<-3;minOS<-30;maxOS<-50

##make mesh
mesh6<-inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain=data1[,c("Lon","Lat")], max.edge = c(minME, maxME), cutoff = co, offset = c(minOS, maxOS))
plot(mesh6)
points(data1[,c("Lon","Lat")])

####The SPDE model is defined with following priors
sig0 = 1;rho0 = 1
spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh6, alpha=2, prior.pc.rho = c(rho0, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(sig0, 0.5))

###projector matrix for known
A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh6, loc = as.matrix(data1[,c("Lon","Lat")]))

###make index for spatial field
s.index<-inla.spde.make.index(name="spatial.field",n.spde=spde$n.spde)

##and the stack data is defined
stk.est <- inla.stack(data=list(y=log(data1$ys+1)),
                      A=list(A,1),
                      effects=list(c(s.index,list(Intercept=1)),
                                   list(data1[,4:ncol(data1)])),
                      tag='est')

##for number of trials in binomial
ntt=rep(1,nrow(data1))

fam1="gaussian"

#####Notice: here I put each covariate into a variate in R, named from "gr01" to "gr99"###
ori<-"y ~ 0 + Intercept"
ori1<-"y ~ 0 + Intercept"
AIC_list<-c()
AIC_best<-0
new<-"gr1"
for (i in seq(1,100,1)){
  print("                                          ")
  print("______________Next Covariate______________")
  print(new)
  form1<-formula(ori1)
  res5<-inla(form1,data=inla.stack.data(stk.est,spde=spde),family=fam1,Ntrials=ntt,control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.est),compute=TRUE,link=1),control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE))
  AIC_list<-c(AIC_list,res5$waic$waic)
  if (i==1){
    AIC_best<-res5$waic$waic
  }
  if (i > 1 & AIC_best-res5$waic$waic>2){
    ori<-ori1
    AIC_best<-res5$waic$waic
  }else{
    print(paste0("!!Covariate    ",get(new),"    not used!!"))
  }
  print(AIC_list)
  print(ori)
  new<-paste0("gr",i)
  ori1<-paste(ori,get(new),sep = " + ")
  print("_________________DONE__________________")
  print("                                          ")
}

form1<-formula(ori)
res5<-inla(form1,data=inla.stack.data(stk.est,spde=spde),family=fam1,Ntrials=ntt,control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk.est),compute=TRUE,link=1),control.compute=list(cpo=TRUE,waic=TRUE))
Efxplot(res5)
```

Thanks!
Chen Yangkang

mostly caused by the observations. covariates should be
scaled/standarized itself, for the same reason but also that without it
you do not control the effect of the priors.

messages.body_plain:
no idea. but using bot 'x' and 'log(x+1)' as covariate, you are kind of
asking for a compromise, as you can write this as

beta1 * x + beta2 * log(1+x) = beta2 * (x + w * log(1+x))

for some weight 'w'. hence you ask, implicitely, to fine the weight 'w'
that makes the 'best covariate', and the sign of w might be negative,
hence the best covariate is some contrast between x and log(1+x).

just a guess
